title: Runtime N operates on separate Development N+1 and never mutates itself
rationale: Separate clones and object stores keep the executable identity a Run trusts distinct from the repository under active development, so self-development cannot silently change the code executing it.

title: Push and Runtime promotion remain maintainer-owned, never automatic
rationale: WFC coordinates only its admitted committed envelope; the maintainer separately reviews, accepts, may push, and may later promote a Runtime, so widening execution authority always requires an explicit human act.

title: Policy determines authority; Profile determines flow; WorkItem bounds task/scope; Coordinator executes deterministically; Agent performs bounded work
rationale: Separating what is allowed (Policy), how work flows (Profile), what is in scope (WorkItem), what executes it (Coordinator), and who performs semantic work (Agent) keeps authority independent of any single agent's self-report.

title: WFC is Level-0 governed bounded execution, not Level-1 project planning or orchestration
rationale: Real DMC work against Core falsified the earlier fractal (self-similar nested loop) hypothesis: Level 0 converges a known, pinned WorkItem, while Level 1 (goal custody, discovery, replanning, cross-session persistence) is unpinned and discovery-driven. WFC intentionally owns only Level 0.

title: Agent requests and self-report do not themselves grant repository authority
rationale: Git and reducer-enforced admitted routes are authority; an agent's requested route, proposed Finding disposition, or scope request is a request the Coordinator may reject. Dogfooding repeatedly exercised this and the reducer held fail-closed every time.

title: Trusted evidence execution is Coordinator-owned; agent-side checks are exploratory only
rationale: Only Coordinator-selected, pinned evidence commands are trusted repository truth; an agent's own shell checks (e.g. a missing bare `python`) are informative to the agent but never substitute for or override trusted evidence.

title: Coordinator hard autonomous-Hop ceiling is independent of WorkItem and RepositoryPolicy budgets
rationale: WorkItem.max_autonomous_hops <= RepositoryPolicy.max_autonomous_hops <= Coordinator hard ceiling is enforced independently at four separate sites (RepositoryPolicy parsing, WorkItem admission, operator preflight, serial-Hop driver), so raising the product ceiling never widens any configured policy or WorkItem by itself.

title: Coordinator hard autonomous-Hop ceiling is currently 20
rationale: Raised from a historical value of 5 (dcb1da0, accepted 9fc478b) to decouple the product ceiling from that coincidentally-equal old value. This repository's own self-development RepositoryPolicy deliberately keeps max_autonomous_hops at 5; the higher ceiling is not itself an authorization to run longer Hop budgets.

title: Provider sandboxing is not claimed as Coordinator-owned containment
rationale: The Codex CLI adapter's `--sandbox workspace-write` request is provider-owned behavior the Coordinator does not verify; treating it as a trusted OS/environment boundary would overclaim a guarantee WFC does not currently provide.

title: WFC Project Memory promotion moves toward a Git-backed review boundary rather than adding locking/transactional exclusivity to the custom staging protocol
rationale: The strong staged-proposal/fingerprint protocol (d201af5) closed the semantic and Make-ordering findings from the first review, but the correction rereview (773ea97) showed its marker-load/compare/write/consume sequence is not an exclusive critical section: two concurrent `memory-promote` processes can both validate and consume one reviewed proposal (14-of-30 double-success). Closing that would require locking, atomic marker claim, or equivalent exclusive-consumption machinery. Concurrent/multi-user promotion is not a current requirement -- Project Memory is maintained by a single maintainer, and uncoordinated simultaneous workbook editing would already need coordination outside memory-promote -- so further transactional machinery is disproportionate. The experiment showed that a strong staged proposal/approval contract naturally grows a second state/identity lifecycle beside Git; WFC will instead simplify toward two persistent representations only (canonical JSON, editable ODS), with Git itself as the proposal/review/acceptance/history/rollback boundary and at most a non-persistent temporary import buffer carrying no proposal identity, approval semantics, fingerprint lifecycle, or lock. The strong-staging implementation and its reviews remain in Git history as evidence for a future use case that genuinely needs multi-user delayed-approval promotion. This simplification is a direction, not yet implemented.
